title: The Two Faces of the Heavenly Prosopon: Love and the Strife Being Refined
arc: From a single heavenly prosopon two faces appear — the face of agape (beauty joined with longing) and the opposite face of love-of-strife — and the teaching shows that the powers of heaven habitually reveal both, refining the second out of themselves on account of the soul mingled in them.
reading:
Although the surviving text is heavily broken, its argument can be followed as a single movement. The teaching takes up what manifests "in the heavens" — that is, in the higher states of the spiritual organism — and observes that what becomes visible there habitually proceeds out of a prosopon, a face. The face here is the established correspondence between an inner state and what it expresses outward. The teaching then makes its decisive move: this single heavenly prosopon is not simple but bears two likenesses, two faces, and from these two the powers of heaven habitually reveal themselves.

The first face is named directly: the face of agape, the face of love, "which is beauty together with longing." This is the proper face of heaven — divine love in its emanating quality, where the beauty of conjunction (the form love takes when it has its object) is inseparable from the longing by which love continually reaches toward that object. Beauty and longing together describe love in its living motion: it is full and yet still desiring, possessing and yet still drawn. This is the face of the Beloved of the Lights as it appears in the powers above.

The second face stands "beside" the first, and the surviving fragment names what is in those who bear it: ⲧⲙⲛⲧⲭⲁⲓ̈ⲙ̄ⲗⲁⲍ — love-of-strife, contentiousness, the affection that opposes agape. The teaching says of this second face that it is something the heavenly powers "habitually refine" — habitually purify out, separate forth. So the two faces are not two equal poles within heaven. The first is heaven's own face. The second is the residue of mingling still present even in the powers above, on account of the soul (the Living Soul) which is in them and which has not yet been wholly extracted. Wherever the Living Soul is present in mingled state, the face of strife can still appear — and wherever the powers of heaven receive that soul, they take up its purification as their continual labor.

The spiritual process being taught is therefore the ongoing refinement carried out at the heavenly level itself. The heavens are not static gallery of finished forms; they are the place where the affection-of-strife borne in by the soul is continuously sorted out from the affection-of-love, the contrary face habitually being refined away so that only the face of agape — beauty-with-longing — remains revealed. The two likenesses together explain why the same heavenly prosopon can show good and bad faces: it is the same surface receiving both the radiance of love and the residue of the mingling, and it is the work of the powers of heaven themselves to keep purifying the second until the first alone shines through.

Because of the lacunae one cannot recover the precise enumeration (the gap at §4541 may have specified "two likenesses" of a particular kind, and §4543 names the love-of-strife without its full predicate), but the shape of the teaching is clear: a single prosopon, two faces, one to be revealed and one to be refined, and the soul as the reason both appear together.
